title: Multi-Head Attention
oneLineScope: Why several attention heads in parallel beat one, and how they are split and recombined.
prose:
The single attention operation from the previous node has a quiet limitation, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. Each row of the attention matrix \(A\) is one probability distribution over positions — one softmax, one weighting, one way of deciding who is relevant to whom. So a position gets exactly one blend of the sequence. But the relations a word participates in are rarely singular. Take the word bank in “the bank by the river raised its rates”: resolving its sense wants the nearby river; resolving what raised means wants its subject several words back; tracking its wants an antecedent. These are different relations over the same tokens, and one distribution cannot encode all of them at once — a single softmax can sharply favor one set of positions or hedge across several, but it cannot simultaneously be peaked on the syntactic head and on the coreferent and on the local modifier. You are asking one mixture to do the work of many. Multi-head attention is the obvious response: run several attention operations in parallel, each free to specialize, then combine what they find.

The idea: split, attend in parallel, recombine

Rather than perform one attention with the full model width, multi-head attention performs \(h\) of them — \(h\) is the number of heads — each in its own lower-dimensional subspace. Every head gets its own learned projections, so each head decides for itself what to match on and what to carry. The heads run independently and in parallel; their outputs are then concatenated back to the full width and passed through one final learned projection that lets the model mix what the heads discovered. The crucial accounting choice is that the per-head width is the full width divided by the number of heads, so the heads partition the representation budget rather than multiplying it. You are not buying more computation; you are spending the same computation as several narrow, specialized lookups instead of one wide, undifferentiated one.

If you want a reference point from your own toolkit: think of a mixture model where each component is fit to explain a different regularity in the data, except here the “components” are attention patterns, the assignment of work to heads is learned by gradient descent rather than by EM, and the final projection is what stitches the per-component contributions back into a single representation.

The math, with dimensions

Let the input be \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per position (\(n\) positions, width \(d_{\text{model}}\)), as before. For each head \(i = 1, \ldots, h\), three learned weight matrices project \(X\) down into that head's subspace:

\[ W_Q^{i}, W_K^{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}, \qquad W_V^{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v} \]

and the head is exactly the scaled dot-product attention of the previous node, applied to those projections:

\[ \operatorname{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(X W_Q^{i},\, X W_K^{i},\, X W_V^{i}) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{(X W_Q^{i})(X W_K^{i})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) X W_V^{i} \]

Each \(\operatorname{head}_i\) is therefore an \(n \times d_v\) matrix: \(n\) output rows, one per position, each of width \(d_v\). The \(h\) heads are concatenated along the width axis and projected once more:

\[ \operatorname{MultiHead}(X) = \operatorname{Concat}(\operatorname{head}_1, \ldots, \operatorname{head}_h)\, W_O, \qquad W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{(h \cdot d_v) \times d_{\text{model}}} \]

The concatenation stacks the \(h\) blocks of width \(d_v\) side by side, giving an \(n \times (h \cdot d_v)\) matrix; the output projection \(W_O\) maps that back to \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\), so the whole block is shape-preserving — it takes \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) in and returns \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) out, which is what lets it stack into a residual stream. Note that \(W_O\) is not cosmetic: without it the concatenation would be a fixed, blockwise partition with no way for information found in one head to inform the channels assigned to another. \(W_O\) is the learned mixing that makes the heads a team rather than a committee filing separate reports.

The original Transformer base model sets these to \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), \(h = 8\), and therefore \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h = 64\). That last equation is the design's load-bearing trick: because each head's width is \(d_{\text{model}}/h\), the total cost of computing all \(h\) heads is approximately the cost of a single attention at the full width \(d_{\text{model}}\). Eight heads of width 64 do roughly the same arithmetic as one head of width 512 — you get the specialization for free, paid for by giving each head a thinner slice rather than by doing more work. (Dividing evenly is a convention, not a law; \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h\) is simply what keeps the budget fixed, and is what the paper uses.)

One more thing the equations hide, worth knowing because it explains why the “split” costs nothing in practice. Writing \(h\) separate projections \(W_Q^{i}\) suggests \(h\) separate matrix multiplies, but no implementation does that. Stacking the per-head matrices side by side gives three full-width matrices \(W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\) (when \(h \cdot d_k = d_{\text{model}}\)); you compute \(XW_Q,\,XW_K,\,XW_V\) once each, then simply reshape the \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) result into \(h\) slices of width \(d_k\) and run the \(h\) attentions as one batched operation. The heads are not really separate computations at all — they are a single wide projection partitioned after the fact, which is precisely why the cost matches one full-width attention and why the split is a bookkeeping decision about how to group the channels, not an architectural surcharge.

What the heads actually learn — and a caveat

The motivating story is that different heads come to track different kinds of relation: one head attends from each token to its syntactic governor, another to the adjacent token, another carries a coreference-like signal linking a pronoun to its antecedent. When researchers visualized the attention matrices of trained models, patterns like these did appear, and they are genuinely suggestive — the picture of heads as specialists is not invented from nothing.

But be careful with how much weight that picture bears. Head “roles” are a post-hoc interpretation of learned weights, read off the attention maps after training, not a property the architecture guarantees or the objective rewards. Nothing in the loss says “head 3 shall do coreference.” Many heads are diffuse, redundant, or hard to label; later work found that a substantial fraction can be pruned with little loss. So treat the clean “syntax head / coreference head” vignettes as illustrative folklore, useful for intuition and partly borne out by inspection, rather than as a specification of what the mechanism does. What the architecture actually guarantees is narrower and solid: \(h\) independent subspaces in which the model can represent \(h\) distinct attention patterns at once, with the optimizer free to use that capacity however lowers the loss.

Where it connects

This is a strict generalization of the single-head scaled dot-product attention you arrived from: set \(h = 1\) and \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}\) (and \(W_O\) the identity) and the block collapses back to one full-width attention. Going forward, multi-head attention is the first of the two sublayers inside the transformer block — wrapped there in a residual connection and layer normalization, and paired with a position-wise feed-forward network. One thing it conspicuously does not supply is any notion of word order: like the single head, it is a sum over an unordered set, which is exactly the gap positional encoding fills.

diagrams.caption: The split-into-heads, attend-in-parallel, concatenate, and project pipeline, with every tensor shape labeled.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline. Input matrix X of shape n by d_model fans out into h parallel heads. Each head i applies its own learned projections W_Q-i, W_K-i, W_V-i to produce per-head queries, keys and values of width d_k or d_v, runs scaled dot-product attention, and emits head-i of shape n by d_v. The h head outputs are concatenated into a matrix of shape n by (h times d_v), then multiplied by the output projection W_O to give a result of shape n by d_model. A note records that d_k equals d_v equals d_model divided by h, so the total compute matches a single full-width attention.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram, left to right, of multi-head attention. On the left, an input matrix labeled X with shape n by d_model, drawn as a short stack of rows. From X, draw h parallel branches into a stack of head boxes; show three of them explicitly — labeled 'head 1', 'head 2', and 'head h' — with a vertical ellipsis between head 2 and head h to indicate the rest. Group the head boxes inside a light rounded enclosure labeled 'h heads in parallel'. Into each head, show its own learned projections with arrows labeled '× W_Q^i', '× W_K^i', '× W_V^i' producing that head's Q and K of shape n by d_k and V of shape n by d_v, feeding a small box labeled 'scaled dot-product attention'; each head emits an output labeled 'head_i' with shape n by d_v. To the right, all head outputs flow into a box labeled 'Concat' producing a matrix of shape n by (h · d_v). An arrow labeled '× W_O' leads from Concat to the final output matrix of shape n by d_model on the far right. Label every matrix with its shape. Add a small margin note with a leader line reading 'd_k = d_v = d_model / h  →  total compute ≈ one full-width attention'. Use the attention color convention: queries blue, keys red, values green. Structural diagram: shapes and flow must be exact.

diagrams.caption: Three heads, one sentence: each head imposes a different attention pattern over the same tokens.
diagrams.altText: The same short sentence 'the bank by the river raised its rates' is shown three times in three stacked rows, one row per head. In each row, arcs connect a focused word to the words that head attends to. Head 1 links adjacent words (a local or positional pattern). Head 2 links the verb raised to its subject bank (a syntactic-dependency pattern). Head 3 links the pronoun its back to bank (a coreference-like pattern). The caption stresses that these labels are an observed, post-hoc interpretation, not a guarantee.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual illustration showing that different attention heads impose different patterns over the SAME sentence. Write the same short sentence three times, stacked in three rows, the tokens spaced out and identical each time: 'the  bank  by  the  river  raised  its  rates'. Label the three rows 'head 1', 'head 2', 'head 3'. In row 1, draw light arcs linking each word to its immediate neighbours, annotated 'attends locally / nearby tokens'. In row 2, draw a prominent arc from 'raised' back to 'bank', annotated 'verb → its subject (syntactic)'. In row 3, draw a prominent arc from 'its' back to 'bank', annotated 'pronoun → antecedent (coreference-like)'. Emphasize that all three are reading the identical tokens but weighting different relations. Add a small caption in muted tone: 'head roles are an observed, post-hoc interpretation — not guaranteed'. No tensor shapes and no equations. Conceptual diagram: intuition over precise labels.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The defining source. §3.2.2 gives the multi-head equations, the Concat–W_O recombination, and the base hyperparameters h = 8, d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64; the note that splitting keeps total cost near a single full-width attention is there too. Half a page; read it once the single-head operation is solid.

The clearest visual account of the split into heads, the parallel attentions, and the concatenate-then-project step. Its worked attention-map figures are also where the 'this head looks at X' intuition is easiest to see — and to take with a grain of salt.

bibliography.citation: Rush, A., et al. "The Annotated Transformer." Harvard NLP.
bibliography.annotation: A line-by-line PyTorch reimplementation of the paper. The MultiHeadedAttention class shows exactly how the per-head projections are packed, how Concat and W_O are realized in code, and how the shapes line up. For the reader who trusts a thing once they have seen it run.

expansion: Deeper treatment the prose deliberately omits, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the exact parameter count and FLOP accounting that makes h heads of width d_model/h cost ≈ one full-width attention — Vaswani §3.2.2; (2) the common implementation that computes all heads at once with single packed projection matrices reshaped to (h, d_k), rather than h separate matmuls (Annotated Transformer); (3) the empirical head-pruning and head-interpretability literature that both supports and qualifies the 'specialist head' story — present as observation, not architecture, and only if a cited source is added for it; (4) why d_k and d_v need not equal d_model/h in general, and what changes if they do not. Cite each claim to its source section; do not introduce results from outside the bibliography.
